questions.short_title: NAEMSP guidance: older adults after low-acuity falls
questions.question: The NAEMSP position statement says 'lift assist' calls involving older adults should be framed how?
options: As routine encounters needing no assessment
As patient encounters warranting full assessment
As uniformly low-acuity minor traumas
As responses only worth tracking at dispatch
questions.explanation: The statement recommends treating these calls as patient encounters warranting assessment for underlying medical causes, injuries and safety, not as minor events. It acknowledges a system-level bias toward underassessment, though the abstract-only caveat means detailed recommendations still can't be fully checked.

questions.short_title: Dispatcher CPR and survival in shockable OHCA
questions.question: The huge survival gap between dispatcher-assisted CPR ongoing at arrival and crew-initiated CPR (30-day survival 54.6% vs 7.1%) should be interpreted mainly as what?
options: Evidence that crew-initiated CPR is harmful
A marker that bystanders had already started CPR early, not a like-for-like comparison
Proof that dispatcher instructions directly cause a near eight-fold survival benefit
Evidence that crews arrive too slowly in shockable arrests
questions.explanation: DA-CPR still running when the crew arrives tells you the bystander started CPR early, which also selects for better-prognosis arrests. The authors flag massive confounding by indication, so this is an association, not a causal effect.

questions.short_title: Prehospital pain assessment happens too rarely
questions.question: Across the studies in this systematic review, how often was pain assessed and documented in the prehospital setting?
options: In 46.7% to 60% of patients
In 22.5% to 46.7% of patients
In more than 50% of patients, matching recommended standards
In up to 22.5% of patients, with some studies under 10%
questions.explanation: The review found pain was assessed and documented in only 22.5% to 46.7% of patients, well below recommended standards. Keep in mind the eight studies were heterogeneous and could not be quantitatively pooled.

questions.short_title: Delays in NSW paediatric trauma retrieval
questions.question: After stabilising the patient at the referring hospital, how often did the specialist paediatric retrieval team take more than 10 minutes to depart?
options: In 55% of missions
In 80% of missions
In about half of missions
In 30% of missions
questions.explanation: Teams took over 10 minutes to leave in 80% of missions, suggesting a consistent delay at the referring hospital once the patient was ready. The data are retrospective, from a single service, and include no patient outcomes, so the clinical impact of these delays is unknown.

questions.short_title: Every minute counts: early bystander CPR
questions.question: A national registry analysis of bystander CPR during the pandemic found overall CPR rates stayed stable. What did the time-to-event analysis reveal that the headline rates missed?
options: Bystander CPR rates rose sharply for witnessed arrests
Early initiation within 10 minutes fell modestly during the pandemic
CPR quality, not timing, worsened during the pandemic
Delay to CPR made no difference to neurological outcomes
questions.explanation: Overall rates were nearly identical (58.7% vs 58.6%), but early starts slipped (aHR 0.96), and CPR begun at 0–3 minutes carried much better odds of favourable neurological outcome than starts after 10 minutes. The timing link is associative, so confounding like dispatch delays can't be ruled out.

questions.short_title: Prehospital qSOFA adds a little prognostic signal
questions.question: A prehospital qSOFA of 2 or more in a suspected infection patient was associated with worse 30-day mortality, but what did the study find about how much it added to what's already known at ED arrival?
options: It was only useful in patients who screened negative at ED triage
It added almost nothing to a model using arrival vitals and labs
It predicted mortality as accurately as the arrival vitals and labs combined
It reclassified most patients into different triage categories
questions.explanation: The prehospital qSOFA stayed associated with death even after adjusting for arrival data, but changed the AUC by only 0.007. It's hypothesis-generating: a single Turkish centre with 58% of eligible patients excluded means serious selection bias, so no change to disposition decisions.

questions.short_title: Prehospital ACS risk stratification: the evidence
questions.question: According to this review, which prehospital ACS risk stratification approach had the strongest evidence for safe field risk assessment?
options: HEART-derived pathways combined with point-of-care troponin testing
AI-assisted ECG interpretation tools
Provider gestalt without any structured tool
Biomarker-free clinical decision rules used on their own
questions.explanation: HEART-derived approaches with point-of-care troponin showed the strongest evidence for safe prehospital risk assessment and reduced healthcare use. AI ECG tools looked promising but haven't been prospectively validated for outcomes, and the review was narrative rather than systematic.

questions.short_title: Burnout linked to suicidal risk in EMS
questions.question: In this cross-sectional survey of EMS professionals, how were burnout, anxiety and depression related to suicidal risk?
options: Each was linked to lower suicidal risk when social support was high
Higher scores on each of these tracked with higher suicidal risk
Only depression was linked to suicidal risk
Burnout was linked to risk, but anxiety and depression were not
questions.explanation: Scores on all burnout domains and the anxiety and depression subscales each corresponded with higher suicidal risk, with elevated risk among gender-diverse respondents. Because the survey was cross-sectional and self-selected, these are associations only and can't show causation.
